Women water seedlings at a nursery near Buee, Ethiopia. Michael Tewelde / AFP via Getty Images

A legacy of deforestation has left Ethiopia struggling with more intense flooding and drought. The country is trying to restore its native forests through one of the world’s most ambitious and well-funded tree-planting campaigns, but experts question whether the trees will survive.

By Samuel Abate and Freddie Clayton • October 1, 2026

Facebook

Twitter

LinkedIn

Email

Niku Argane’s farm sits on a steep hillside in central Ethiopia’s semi-mountainous Gurage Zone, where years of flooding have carved deep gullies through the land. Soil that once produced enough barley and potatoes to feed his wife and four children — and left a surplus to sell in the market — has eroded, while drought has made what land remains harder to cultivate.

“We have never stopped farming, but our production declined because of land degradation,” the 32-year-old said from his farm in Ambele Kebele.

Over the last century, Ethiopia nearly eradicated its forests as trees were cleared for farming, grazing, and fuel. The loss of tree cover and tree roots allowed wind and rain to wash away fertile topsoil and contributed to declining crop yields. That vulnerability is now being compounded by climate change. Ethiopia is among the countries most vulnerable to its effects: Heavier downpours are sluicing away depleted soils and triggering landslides, while more intense droughts, combined with the loss of shade that trees once provided, rapidly dry out the land.

Land degradation costs the country an estimated $4.3 billion a year through smaller harvests and lost income to farmers, which also means there is less food to eat. With more than 100 million Ethiopians dependent on agriculture for their livelihoods, the consequences reach far beyond the environment. Climate shocks and crop losses are among the biggest drivers of acute hunger; in 2024, 15.8 million Ethiopians were estimated to need food assistance, roughly 12 percent of the population.

Reforestation almost always fails, says a researcher, but even if 30 percent of trees planted in Ethiopia survive, “it’s still huge.”

Now the country is trying to reverse this trajectory. Argane planted 80 tree seedlings on his farmland and another 50 in a communal area — a small contribution to a vastly larger effort. In just the last seven years, tens of millions of Ethiopians have planted more than 47 billion seedlings across the country in one of the world’s largest environmental restoration campaigns. Volunteers for the program, which aims to plant 50 billion seedlings by 2030, are planting trees to rebuild native forests and integrating them into farmland. In the process, they are sequestering carbon to help protect future generations from ever more extreme weather.

Such programs often fall short, but Ethiopians are finding hope in the scale of their ambitions. “Reforestation is one of the most difficult things you can imagine,” said Aad Kessler, a researcher at the Netherlands’ Wageningen University. “It almost always fails, but this is so big that even if 30 percent of the trees survive, it’s still huge.”

In the early 20th century, forests covered an estimated 35 to 40 percent of Ethiopia. Its highlands were greener, with forests spanning much of the country’s cool, fertile uplands. But as populations grew and settlements spread, trees were cleared for agriculture, pasture, fuel, and construction. As soils lost their fertility, cultivation moved onto increasingly marginal land, including steep slopes, where tillage and the loss of protective vegetation led to the erosion of fertile topsoil, which washed into rivers and reservoirs. By 1989, forest cover was estimated at less than 3 percent , while Ethiopia’s highlands were losing around 1 billion metric tons of topsoil every year.

Farms in North Gondar in the Ethiopian highlands. The spread of agriculture has stripped the region of trees. Danita Delimont Creative

After the devastating droughts and famines of the 1970s and 1980s, Ethiopia’s government and international donor organizations began investing heavily in soil and water conservation, excluding livestock from worn-out land, planting trees across the country, and building terraces and check dams — small, low barriers of rocks and logs placed across gullies — to slow the flow of rainwater. By the 2000s, restoration programs were being implemented at increasing scale.

The government supercharged that effort in 2019 by turning tree-planting into a nationwide campaign with a scheme known as the Green Legacy Initiative, which mobilized millions of individuals and groups, including farmers, public servants, schools, and religious organizations, and distributed free seedlings across the country. In 2024, the government established the Green Legacy and Landscape Restoration Special Fund, committing 0.5 percent to 1 percent of the annual federal budget — roughly $73 million to $145 million — to restoring landscapes. It was an unusually large commitment for a low-income country, and the program’s success and ambition, according to development experts, contributed to the selection of Ethiopia as the host of next year’s U.N. climate conference — a prestigious honor that will help the nation showcase its greening efforts.

You can’t expect a baby to grow if you don’t care for it, says an ecologist, but “that’s how plantation in Ethiopia is being done.”

In August, 26.6 million Ethiopians planted 800 million tree seedlings in a single day, according to government figures , beating the previous year’s tally of 714.7 million . One of the volunteers, Yeshihareg Teferi, traveled at sunrise from her home in Addis Ababa to Tulu Dimtu so she could hunch in the rain to dig holes in the mud. It was Teferi’s fifth year participating in the annual event. Previously she’d planted indigenous species, including African wild olive and African fern pine. This time, she chose juniper. “We have a responsibility to ensure future generations inherit a green and fertile environment, rather than barren land,” she said.

There are already signs the work is having an impact.

The government reports that national forest cover rose from 17.2 percent in 2019 to 23.6 percent in 2023, while studies of restored areas have found substantial reductions in soil erosion. Between 2013 and 2023, the annual deforestation rate fell from more than 350 square miles to around 100 square miles.

Volunteers plant seedlings on the outskirts of Addis Ababa as part of a nationwide tree-planting drive in early August.

Such efforts can also benefit wildlife. In Abijata-Shalla National Park, in the Ethiopian highlands, workers replanted degraded areas and built terraces and contour bunds (small earthen ridges that run across hillsides to slow runoff and allow water to soak into the soil). As trees and native grasses returned, more water infiltrated into the ground, and water levels on lakes in the park began to rise, said Kumera Wakjira, director-general of the Ethiopian Wildlife Conservation Authority. More water spurred the return of fish and fish-eating birds like cormorants and African darters. Grant’s gazelles and wild dogs are also expanding into areas where they were previously scarce, Wakjira said.

But planted trees are not guaranteed to survive. A 2022 study of 176 reforestation projects in Asia found that around half of planted trees did not live five years. And trees alone do not make a forest, said Endalkachew Wolde-Meskel, a soil scientist and senior researcher at the Center for International Forestry Research: That process usually requires the regeneration of grasses and other vegetation, in addition to soil- and water-conservation measures and management by local communities. “The objective is not really ‘plant trees,’” he said. “It is to restore the functioning of the entire landscape.”

Emiru Birhane Hizikias, an Ethiopian restoration ecologist at Norway’s Nord University, said it was a “blessing, politically speaking,” to have the prime minister lead on tree planting but that the scale of the Green Legacy Initiative had outpaced the systems needed to make it work effectively on the ground. Too often, he said, the focus is on getting huge numbers of seedlings into the earth rather than ensuring their survival. You can’t expect a baby to grow if you don’t care for it, he said, but “that’s how plantation in Ethiopia is being done.”

Climate change has already complicated the most basic requirement of restoration: getting seedlings to survive their first season.

Abreham Berta Aneseyee, an environmental scientist at Ethiopia’s Wolkite University and an adviser to the Ministry of Agriculture, disputes that characterization, saying the planting campaign is accompanied by practical advice from government experts in forestry and farming. The experts go from farm to farm, advising smallholders on how to plant and care for different types of seedlings, he said, including how deeply to place them in soil and how to conserve soil with structures like bunds. They also advise farmers on managing forests and protecting trees rather than cutting them down.

A 2026 study of more than 44,500 seedlings planted in southern Ethiopia under the Green Legacy Initiative in 2023 found that about 80 percent had survived, with rates significantly higher among older seedlings, wet-season plantings, and seedlings whose planters had received training in best “plantation practices.” In Humbo and Boloso Sore districts in Ethiopia’s southwestern Wolaita Zone, the Green Legacy Initiative has been layered onto longer-running efforts to sustainably manage land, with communities building check dams to stabilize gullies, digging half-moon ditches to trap water and let it soak into the soil, and planting trees alongside grasses and other vegetation.

Left: Half-moon ditches trap runoff, helping to nourish plants and combat erosion. Right: A check dam in a gully stems erosion by slowing the flow of water. Courtesy of the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT

Ethiopia’s approach has few direct parallels in Africa for its combination of political leadership, funding, public mobilization, and scale, said Kessler of Wageningen University. He compared the effort with China’s restoration of the Loess Plateau, one of the world’s most highly eroded regions. In the 1990s, China launched major restoration efforts on the plateau, including a World Bank-backed watershed rehabilitation project and, starting in 1999, the Grain for Green program, which paid farmers to restrict cultivation and plant trees, shrubs, and grasses. By 2016, more than 11,500 square miles of rain-fed cropland had been converted to more dense forest or grassland, contributing to a 25 percent increase in vegetative cover in a decade.

The comparison has limits, though. China paid farmers to take degraded slopes out of cultivation, while millions of Ethiopian smallholders still depend on the land for food and livelihoods. But Kessler said the two efforts shared a fundamental approach: “Do it massively, and then see where you end up.”

Kessler’s work, which includes a government-backed field project in Ethiopia, takes a more participatory approach, involving farmers and communities in decisions about what to restore and how. “Of course it is better [than top-down action],” he said, “but it takes more time.”

Even as Ethiopia invests in rebuilding forests and soils, climate change is altering the conditions landscapes must withstand. In the arid pastoral regions of Afar and Somali, the Green Legacy Initiative focuses on drought-tolerant species, but it is unclear whether the trees planted today will be able to withstand the conditions they face decades from now.

Volunteers search for bodies in the aftermath of a 2024 landslide in the Geze Gofa district in southern Ethiopia. Michele Spatari / AFP via Getty Images

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change projects more frequent and intense rainfall in East Africa as global temperatures rise. In July 2024, exceptionally heavy rainfall in Ethiopia’s Geze Gofa district, in the southern highlands, triggered two landslides that killed at least 257 people. Recent studies also suggest that climate change is making El Niños more frequent and severe, with consequences for East Africa. This summer, the Famine Early Warning Systems Network linked El Niño to “historically poor” summer rains in parts of Ethiopia, leaving some areas with their driest June and July on record.

For some farmers, the changing climate has already complicated the most basic requirement of restoration: getting seedlings to survive their first season. Belayneh Mamo, 65, a farmer from Ethiopia’s northern and drought-prone Amhara region, relies on July rainfall for his teff, sorghum, maize, and wheat for bulgur. He also receives government-provided coffee, neem, and gesho seeds, but was unable to plant any crop until August, when the season’s first rains arrived.

“In previous years, September was a period when crops were already developing and food such as bulgur and maize were becoming available for consumption,” he said. “The delays affected the seedlings we plant, our crops, and the availability of animal feed.”

On Argane’s hillside in the Gurage Zone, however, signs of restoration are already visible. Since 2019, he has planted grass, fodder, fenugreek, and fruit trees along the edges of his fields, helping to hold soil in place while providing feed for the four cows, six goats, and three sheep that he keeps for milk and meat. His barley harvest has risen from about 1,800 pounds per acre to roughly 3,200, while the trees and grasses have reduced erosion and slowed the flow of water across his land during heavy rains.

“Restoring degraded land isn’t just about protecting the environment,” Argane said. “It’s also about making life better for my family and community.”

Watch: Kemi Badenoch says she wants Reform voters to "come back"

Published 6 October 2026

Kemi Badenoch has said she would rather have another general election than do a deal with Reform UK to secure power, if no party wins the next election.

The Conservative Party leader told the BBC that Nigel Farage's Reform are "neck deep in scandal" and joining forces with them would "just be one problem after another".

Polling suggests there would be a hung parliament at the next election, with Labour currently expected to be the largest party followed by Reform and the Tories.

As the Conservative Party conference in Birmingham nears its end, Badenoch has also pledged to cut the cost of hiring 21 to 24-year-olds by halving the rate of employer national insurance (NI) contributions.

Badenoch has been trying to position the Conservatives as a party that is different to the one that suffered an historic defeat in the 2024 general election.

She told BBC Political Editor Chris Mason "we are going back to the authentic Conservative Party, that people knew and loved" after she published a 100-page document, called The Right Way, setting out the party's principles , external .

Badenoch added "politics is volatile", as she tried to talk up the party's chances despite the polls suggesting only one-in-five voters would back them.

She said: "We're in a different political world, and it is within that context that we know that we can win. I'm not saying that we would win.

"The current polling shows a hung parliament, no party getting an overall majority.

"My prediction is that there would be another election immediately after. But we're the only credible alternative to Labour, the only ones with a plan."

A scenario was put to Badenoch in which the Conservatives would be the largest party and Reform have a significant presence in a hung parliament after the next election.

Asked if she would work with Reform in government, Badenoch replied: "If you want Conservative, you have to vote Conservative. I have said we'd have another election if there was no overall majority."

Badenoch added she wants Reform voters to "come back" to the Conservatives, saying people in Farage's party are "neck deep in scandal, it'd just be one problem after another".

She pointed to the arrest of Dan Thomas, who quit last month as Reform's leader in Wales after he was arrested on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour . Thomas said he had "done nothing wrong".

Badenoch also highlighted the case of Nathan Gill, the former leader of Reform in Wales who was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison after admitting taking bribes for pro-Russia interviews and speeches .

Farage has faced intense scrutiny over financial support he has received , including a £5m gift he received from a billionaire Reform donor before he became an MP. He has insisted he has done nothing wrong.

Badenoch added: "I want to get this economy growing, I want to make the country richer, I want to stop the boats, we've got a plan on borders, we've got a plan on welfare, we've got a plan on defence and bringing energy costs down.

"That's what we're about."

Privately, senior Conservatives talk of what they see as the importance of a potential 'tipping point' in support for the Conservatives and support for Reform UK.

Tories hope that if they can draw level and then establish a small lead over Reform in opinion polls, they can begin to make the case that they are the only viable alternative to Labour winning the next general election, potentially then attracting more support.

Badenoch has long said she wouldn't do a deal with Reform before the election, as it was a party trying to destroy the Conservatives.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said last month he was not tempted to call an early general election , arguing it would throw "the country into a backward-looking process". The next one must be held by August 2029.

Farage has previously said Reform have "replaced the old fuddy-duddy existing Conservative Party" .

To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

Young Tories asked if their party should do a deal with Reform UK

In her speech to the Conservative Party conference on Tuesday, Badenoch is expected to say growing the economy "will be the central organising principle of the next Conservative government" if her party wins power.

She will contrast her approach with that of Burnham's government, accusing Labour of "reckless" spending, adding billions to the national debt and increasing taxes.

Pitching the fight against Labour as "a battle for the soul of this nation", she will argue her party is "a renewed Conservative Party fighting again for the belief that what people earn belongs to them, not government".

Elsewhere in her BBC interview, Badenoch said she was making changes to a policy for young people and was now proposing cutting the rate of employer National Insurance (NI) on earnings from 15% to 7.5% for those aged 21 to 24.

The Tories announced last year that young people would see the first £5,000 of NI they would have paid in their first job redirected into a nominated savings account of their choice.

The party said the policy, dubbed the "First Job Bonus", would have cost £2.8bn a year.

On Tuesday, Badenoch said youth unemployed has "skyrocketed" and "you can't give people a first jobs bonus if they're not getting a first job".

She added: "We're adapting and updating our policy so that it works for the problems they have today."

The Conservatives said the new policy is targeted at starter jobs and the standard rate would apply to earnings above £50,270.

They added it "smooths the cliff edge" which exists as employer NI goes from 0% to the full rate when a worker turns 21.

The government has faced calls to reduce employer NI contributions for younger workers to help boost job opportunities. Around one million young people in the UK are not in education, employment or training.

Asked why the Conservatives were not proposing to cut NI for everyone, Badenoch said: "We have to find the money first.

"So we have a golden economic rule. We are being fiscally credible. We find savings and then we spend it.

"If I could afford to cut it for everybody, I promise you that I would. But young people have a much worse problem than everybody else."

A Labour Party spokesperson said the NI announcement was "more fantasy economics from the Tories", adding the party had "allowed nearly one million of the next generation to be locked out of work or training".

stories.title: Badenoch's £10bn air defence plan points to growing concern over protecting UK's skies
stories.summary: The government and the Conservatives both agree the UK needs better air defences in an increasingly dangerous world.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Current air-defence systems include the Sky Sabre but defence chiefs have warned more is needed

Published 6 October 2026

America and Israel's war with Iran has shown that even the world's most sophisticated air defences can be overwhelmed by enemy missiles and drones, if fired in significant numbers.

Iran's have broken through the layered air defences of US military bases in the Middle-East causing significant damage.

Russia's war in Ukraine has also exposed the huge challenge of defending their own skies from large-scale attacks.

The government's Strategic Defence Review, published in 2025, explicitly warned of the threats to the UK – including ballistic and cruise missiles and drones – and highlighted the need for the UK to invest more in its air defences.

The Labour government is allocating up to £1bn to address it.

The Conservatives now say they will spend more - £10 bn - over a decade. Both parties agree that the UK needs layers of air defences.

Tories pledge £10bn for British anti-missile defence system Published 18 hours ago

Currently the country has a number of systems to deal with short and medium-range threats – from drones to cruise missiles. But the armed forces still lack a weapons system to deal with long-range ballistic and hypersonic missiles.

And those don't come cheap. Each interceptor used by the US Patriot missile system costs about $4m (£3m).

Sophisticated air defences that can deal with a range of threats are expensive. The US Army alone wants to increase its budget for both missiles and interceptors by fourfold next year – to $36bn (£27.1bn).

Israel also spends a significant proportion of its $45bn (£33.9bn) annual military budget on air defences.

For the Conservatives there's also a presentation problem. Their original press release mentioned building a new air defence systems that would be "in essence, a British Iron Dome", referencing Israel's elaborate air defence system .

But any comparison of the challenge of defending Britain's skies with Israel's, about 10% the size of the UK, is naive.

Nor is the threat the same. Israel has regularly been targeted by drones and missiles over the past decade. The UK has not.

The Conservatives now suggest the phrase "Iron Dome" was just a shorthand for better air defences. But even the words "Britannia Shield" may be a misnomer.

It would be nigh on impossible for the UK to develop an air-defence system that could defend the whole country with such limited resources.

At best it could afford a system to protect some key strategic sites – including military bases. At present the UK doesn't even have that.

How much money are other countries spending on air defences?

By BBC Verify

Nick Forienza, a defence analyst from Janes, a military think tank, said the money committed by the government to missile defence under the Defence Investment Plan "is only a fraction of what other countries have declared".

He said the Conservatives' plan to invest £10bn "sounds comparable to what other small countries are doing".

He continued: "Not as small as the Netherlands or Belgium, but let's say Germany or Turkey and now the Greeks are working on something called Achilles Shield.

"That's the kind of magnitude [spending £10bn] that would be required for a serious missile defence system."

Germany is leading the European Sky Shield Initiative (ESSI), a 24‑nation effort to jointly procure air and missile defence systems (IRIS‑T, Patriot, Arrow 3).

Berlin has committed roughly €4bn (£3.4bn) for Arrow 3 alone and is also part of a €5.1bn (£4.3bn) plan to share up to 1,000 Patriot GEM‑T interceptors with Romania, Spain and the Netherlands.

In France, budgets show an "Air and Air Defence" spend of about €4.4bn (£3.7bn) in 2026, but this covers all air force air defence activities, not just missile defence.

Poland, which spends more on defence as a share of its economy than the UK, is building an air and missile defence system worth more than PLN 200bn (£39bn) which will be spent over a number of years.

stories.title: Why Tories are talking about winning the next election
stories.summary: Kemi Badenoch is more popular than her party right now - Tories are hoping it will rub off on them.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The Tories are in an upbeat mood at their annual conference

Published 6 October 2026

Political party conferences can be weird events - where positive thinking and hopeful rhetoric can crowd out reality.

If you spend enough time drinking and socialising with like-minded people anything can seem possible.

That could be one explanation for the upbeat mood of this year's Conservative gathering in Birmingham.

On the face of it, the party has made little progress since it was emphatically ejected from power in 2024. If an election was held tomorrow, it would do even worse than it did back then, according to some polls.

Yet senior figures, including leader Kemi Badenoch, are talking about winning the next general election outright and forming a government.

One reason for their optimism is that they appear to have seen off, for now, the threat of being destroyed or swallowed up by Reform UK - a prospect which hung over last year's conference amid swirling rumours of defections and speculation about deals with Nigel Farage.

Another is Badenoch herself, who appears to have made a positive impression on the public.

Kemi Badenoch puts the finishing touches to her conference speech

Her approval rating has soared in recent months and she is now one of only two party leaders with a net positive rating (the other being Prime Minister Andy Burnham), according to pollsters More In Common. , external

In a presentation to a packed fringe meeting, More In Common's Luke Tryl said the Tory leader is seen as a "breath of fresh air" by focus groups, with many voters on the right describing her as someone unafraid to "say it as it is".

In particular, her punchy performances at Prime Minister's Questions have made a strong impression, earning plaudits such as "intelligent", "professional" and "principled" from those who have seen her in action, according to Tryl.

But like Burnham, Badenoch's personal popularity has yet to transfer to her party, he added, with the Tories being seen as "outdated" and "divided".

It was not all gloom – in contrast to his presentation at last year's Tory conference – and there were "signs of recovery", Tryl said, with a large pool of voters out there who might consider voting Tory, under the right circumstances.

Conservatives freely admit the problem they have got is that voters don't trust them to deliver on any of their promises, when they had 14 years in government to do something about the problems they now say are so pressing.

"Of course, Kemi's ahead of us, we know that," Conservative chairman Kevin Hollinrake told the More in Common meeting.

"Because people do trust Kemi and they don't trust us, that's how I would put it in a nutshell.

"But we are building on that."

Badenoch answers the trust question by saying that the party is under new management now.

She has ditched some of the "culture war" rhetoric and is focusing hard on the economy, and setting out her guiding principles, which amount to a return to old-school Conservatism.

She is not saying that the party could win an election outright if it was held now, arguing that no one could.

But she has ruled out governing with Reform UK in a hung parliament, telling the BBC she would rather hold another election .

Hollinrake sounded a cautious note at the More In Common fringe.

"We are not where we need to be right now. We don't want an election right now, ideally. Ideally, it would come way down the track."

But deputy leader Alex Burghart was quick to stress that the party is making every effort to ensure it is ready for a snap election.

"We are preparing for an election now," he told the meeting.

"We are convinced we can win the election outright."

I'd rather have another election than do a deal with Reform UK, says Badenoch Published 8 hours ago

Tories pledge £10bn for British anti-missile defence system Published 18 hours ago

Shadow chancellor vows to cut at least one tax in every Tory budget Published 1 day ago

He claimed the Tories were more united than at any time in their recent history, with the possible exception of the aftermath of Boris Johnson's 2019 victory.

But they still trail Reform by four or five points in the polls and are as much as nine points behind Labour.

The next challenge for the party, former Scottish Conservative leader Dame Ruth Davidson said, was to become one of the "top two".

At that point, voters who want to see the back of Labour would start moving to the Tories in serious numbers, she argued.

Tactical voting could prove crucial at the next election, whenever it comes, with many people voting to keep parties out of power rather than for who they want to win.

The Tories think they have a strong hand here too.

"For the first time in history, the Conservative Party is now the least hated political party in the country," declared Hollinrake, to laughter and applause.

"When it comes to tactical voting, that's really important."

Not the most inspiring rallying cry you will hear at a party conference, perhaps, but it is grounded in reality.

stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Track UK's latest migration numbers - net migration, visas, asylum and small boats

Published 27 November 2025

Updated 6 October 2026

UK net migration has dropped to the lowest level, outside of the Covid pandemic, since 2012.

How does that sit alongside other key migration measures, including asylum applications, small boat arrivals and visas granted?

Scroll down to find out more about the latest key figures, and get answers to key questions on a range of topics.

UK migration data at a glance

Net migration (change in population), January 2025 to December 2025

Immigration (people arriving), January 2025 to December 2025

Emigration (people leaving), January 2025 to December 2025

Asylum applications, July 2025 to June 2026

Returns and deportations from the UK, July 2025 to June 2026

Arrivals by small boat, 1 January 2026 to 5 October 2026

Small boat crossings and other illegal arrivals

Between 1 January and 5 October 2026, a total of 20,478 people crossed the English Channel by small boat from France. This was down by 40% on the same period the previous year.

These crossings have become the most common way for people to be detected entering the UK illegally since 2020.

Nearly all those who arrive by small boat claim asylum. Under international law, this means they are allowed to stay in the country while their asylum application is considered.

Small boat arrivals made up 40% of asylum applications between July 2025 to June 2026.

Boats that arrived in the UK from 6 October 2025 to 5 October 2026 carried an average of 68 people. This has more than doubled since 2021.

Experts say overcrowding in boats makes crossings riskier . At least 84 people died while attempting to cross the Channel in 2024, according to the United Nations (UN).

When looking at the scale of small boats crossings, the number of these arrivals is about 5% of the size of total immigration into the UK from January 2025 to December 2025.

The government has pledged to “smash the gangs” behind these crossings in order to reduce the numbers.

People from Eritrea accounted for 18% of all arrivals from July 2025 to June 2026.

In the latest figures covering January 2025 to December 2025, at least 2,335 people who arrived by small boat were found to be potential victims of human trafficking or other forms of modern slavery, according to the Home Office.

Another 4,712 people were detected entering the UK without permission via other methods including hiding in vehicles, travelling on ferries or through airports from July 2025 to June 2026. This was down by 17% on the same period the previous year.

There are also individuals who arrive legally, for example via a work or study visa, and then overstay their limit.

The total number of people who live in the UK illegally after arriving legally is not known.

Asylum applications and hotels

An asylum seeker is someone who wants to be in the UK because they say they cannot live safely in their own country due to persecution or violence.

The government must house an asylum seeker if they cannot financially support themselves while their claim is being considered. There were 89,089 people in asylum accommodation as of June 2026.

About 18% of those people, 16,021, were in hotels. These are used when there is not enough shared housing available, such as houses of multiple occupation (HMOs) or former military sites .

The government has pledged to stop the use of hotels by 2029.

More people are in hotels across the south of England than elsewhere in the UK, while HMOs are more common in the north of England and Scotland.

A modern browser with JavaScript and a stable internet connection is required to view this interactive

Type in a postcode or the name of a local council below to see how many asylum seekers are housed in the area

A total of 85,891 people applied for asylum in the UK from July 2025 to June 2026. This was down by 21% on the same period in the previous year.

Most people who arrive in the UK by small boat claim asylum, but they were only 40% of all asylum seekers from July 2025 to June 2026.

The rest include people who arrived by other illegal means or who came to the UK legally and applied for asylum while holding, or just after holding, a valid visa.

It can take years for the government to decide whether someone should be granted asylum.

In June 2026, 40,168 people - across 32,401 asylum applications - were waiting for an initial decision. The number of people awaiting an initial decision was down by 56% on the previous year.

As of June 2026, a further 90,341 refused asylum applications were part of a second backlog, waiting the outcome of an appeal in the courts. This was up by 51% on the previous year.

Together, these initial decision and appeal cases form the government’s total asylum applications backlog, which it has pledged to clear .

Refugee status was granted in about 38% of asylum decisions made by the Home Office from July 2025 to June 2026.

About 39% of asylum appeal cases concluded between January 2026 to December 2026 resulted in a previous refusal decision being overturned.

Returns and deportations from the UK

The government requires people who are in the UK, but no longer have permission to live or work in the country, to leave.

This is called a return and can happen voluntarily or involuntarily.

People can lose the right to be in the UK for different reasons, such as a visa expiring, an asylum claim being refused, or by receiving a criminal conviction that results in deportation.

There were 40,605 returns from July 2025 to June 2026. This was up by 8% on the same period the previous year.

That number of returns is equivalent to about 6% of total emigration from the UK from January 2025 to December 2025.

Of all returns from July 2025 to June 2026:

5,962 had been convicted of a criminal offence 12,568 had lodged an asylum claim at some point 3,310 had arrived in the UK by small boat

People from India made up 27% of all returns from July 2025 to June 2026.

The UK is trialing a scheme with France to return people who arrived in the country on a small boat.

For every person the UK sends back to France, the UK will accept an equal number of asylum seekers.

This is called the "one in, one out" deal. As of 30 June 2026, 1,087 people have been returned through this arrangement.

Returns can happen in different ways. "Enforced returns", which includes deportations, means the government arranges transport to return people to a different country. In some cases, people are escorted by officers.

All other returns are "voluntary". This means a person has agreed to leave and may receive government help with travel and other costs to help facilitate the return.

Some people classed as leaving the country voluntarily do so completely independently and without any government knowledge or involvement .

Independent returns made up 34% of the total from July 2025 to June 2026.

Visas for legal migration

Most people who come to the UK do so legally, after being granted a visa before they travel.

A visa gives someone permission to enter or stay in the UK for a specific purpose, such as work, study or joining family members.

There were 727,487 people who came to the UK via visas from July 2025 to June 2026, not including visitors or people transiting through the UK. This was down by 15% on the same period the previous year.

That does not mean all those people travelled to the UK, only that they were approved to do so.

The most common type of visa people came to the UK on was study, which made up 53% of all visa entries from July 2025 to June 2026.

People from China were the most common group to come to the UK on study visas, making up 23% of the total.

Together, people from China and India accounted for nearly half of all study visas. This has been the case for many years.

Migration to Europe

The EU and UK monitor the number of people crossing borders in the Mediterranean and English Channel by sea without permission.

There were 139,288 sea arrivals to the UK, Greece, Italy, Spain and Cyprus from August 2025 to July 2026.

Crossings to the UK accounted for about 22% of the combined total.

Sea arrivals into mainland Europe peaked in 2015, when the UN said more than a million people crossed the Mediterranean.

The top three countries with the most people claiming asylum from April 2025 to March 2026 were Spain with 133,795, Italy with 124,740 and France with 111,320.

The UK ranked at number five for asylum claims over the same period when compared with 26 other European countries with populations over one million.

When adjusted for population size, the UK ranks at number 10 for asylum applications per 100,000 people.

Net migration measures the overall change in a country’s population due to migration over a given period. It is everyone coming into the country (immigration) minus everyone who leaves (emigration).

The latest available data to compare the UK with other European nations is January 2024 to December 2024.

At that point, the countries with the biggest increase in their population were Spain with 626,000, Germany with 494,000 and the UK with 331,000, after taking into account the people who left the country, and those who arrived.

When adjusting for population size, the UK was in position 11 for increase in population due to migration, alongside 13 other European countries with comparable data per 100,000 residents.

Is the government meeting its pledges on illegal immigration and asylum? Published 26 February

Why do Channel migrants want to come to the UK? Published 9 July 2025

Find out more about people crossing the Channel in small boats Published 22 October 2025

Produced by: Rob England, Libby Rogers, Jess Carr, Aidan McNamee, John Walton, Becky Dale, Allison Shultes, Chris Kay, Steven Connor and Scott Jarvis.

Graphics by: Jez Frazer, Zoe Bartholomew and Joy Roxas

About the data

Figures from government and other official sources can be revised between publications. This page shows data as presented in the latest available release.

Immigration, emigration and net migration

*The net migration figure for the UK will not exactly equal immigration minus emigration because the Office for National Statistics (ONS) publishes it as a rounded number.

Immigration and emigration estimates , external from the ONS are updated twice a year.

Net migration figures use the internationally recognised definition of a long-term migrant: "A person who moves to a country other than that of their usual residence for at least a year."

Visas for legal migration

The total number of visa entries only includes visas that have been granted. It does not include visitor visas or transit visas, where the UK is not the final destination.

Visa figures record when permission was granted, not when or whether someone arrived in the UK.

If a person was granted more than one visa within the year shown, each visa is counted separately.

Work visas refer to new individuals granted permission, or extensions of existing permission. This includes categories such as seasonal work, health and care, domestic worker and youth mobility visas.

Study visas include all individuals sponsored by approved UK education providers, as well as those on short-term study visas.

Family visas allow someone to come to or remain in the UK to live with close family members already here. This includes joining a spouse, partner, child or parent, or coming to care for a relative.

The "Other" category includes visas outside work, study and family routes. This covers humanitarian schemes such as the Ukraine Sponsorship Scheme and the British National (Overseas) route. It also includes family permits for people from European Union or European Economic Area countries.

Asylum applications and accommodation

Home Office figures for asylum seekers in hotels are published under the category "contingency accommodation - hotel".

The number of people in all other forms of accommodation includes non-hotel contingency accommodation, as well as initial, dispersal and "other" accommodation.

To show how evenly accommodation is distributed, a scale compares each local authority's share of people in that type of accommodation with the UK-wide average for areas using the same accommodation type:

Less than half – more than 50% below the average share

Lower than – between 25% and 50% below the average share

About the same as – within 25% of the average share

Higher than – between 25% and 100% above the average share

More than double – more than 100% above the average share

Backlog figures for people waiting for an initial asylum decision include both main applicants and dependants.

Open appeals against refused asylum applications refer to individuals. Figures on appeals are published every three months by the Ministry of Justice, at a different time from other government asylum statistics. It also includes a small number of appeals against revocation of protection.

Small boat crossings and other irregular arrivals

Small boat crossing figures and the average number of people per boat are taken from the Home Office daily data , external .

Entering the UK without permission is an offence under immigration law , external , but asylum seekers are generally not prosecuted if they claim asylum on arrival. In some cases, people have been prosecuted alongside other offences, such as people smuggling or re-entering after deportation.

The International Organization for Migration (IOM) collects figures on people who have died , external or gone missing while crossing from mainland Europe to the UK. These reports are based on information from French and UK officials (such as police or coastguard) and media sources. The IOM considers them an undercount because there are no official statistics.

The figures may include people who died in the Channel itself, as well as those who died while travelling to a crossing point.

Data on modern slavery includes final decisions only. Modern slavery covers human trafficking, slavery, servitude and forced labour.

Figures for other entries without permission combine all recorded irregular arrivals that were not by small boat. This includes inadequately documented air arrivals, recorded detections at UK ports, and other recorded detections within the UK.

Returns and deportations

People who are denied entry at the border and then leave the UK are not included in the returns figures on this page.

Returns involving the government are grouped into three categories. Enforced returns (which include deportations) are cases where the Home Office requires someone to leave and arranges their removal, usually because they have no legal right to remain or following a criminal conviction.

Assisted voluntary returns are when someone agrees to leave the UK and receives government support, such as help with travel documents, flights or reintegration assistance.

Controlled voluntary returns are when someone leaves the UK voluntarily without being forcibly removed, but their departure is formally recorded by the Home Office.

Independent returns are referred to by the government as "other verified returns," and refer to individuals who have left the UK without

People returned after a criminal conviction include non-British citizens convicted in the UK of any criminal offence, or convicted abroad of a serious criminal offence.

UK migration compared with other countries

Sea arrival figures are taken from the UNHCR European sea arrivals dashboard and combined with UK Home Office small boat data.

Asylum application, immigration and emigration figures for European countries are the latest available data from Eurostat for: Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, Czechia, Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Slovakia, Slovenia, Bulgaria, Romania, Norway, Switzerland and Croatia.

UK population figures are from ONS, National Records of Scotland and the Northern Ireland Statistics and Research Agency 2024 mid-year estimates. European population figures are from Eurostat as of 1 January 2024.

To ensure comparability with the UK, European countries with populations under one million are excluded from per-capita comparisons of net migration and asylum applications.

For net migration comparisons, only countries that include asylum seekers or refugees in their immigration figures are included.

These are: Austria, Belgium, Estonia, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Netherlands, Norway, Slovenia, Spain and Switzerland.

Portugal was also excluded as it did not have net migration data available for 2024, it will be re-included in future updates.

Published 6 October 2026

Queen Camilla has paid tribute to the bestselling author and former politician Jeffrey Archer, who has died at the age of 86.

"Seldom does an author get to live a life as rich, varied and colourful as any of the characters in their books, or with as many surprising plot twists," the Queen said in a statement.

She added that Archer was "not without flaw", but that "friends will recall him as an irrepressible life force through all the many differing chapters of his life".

The former Conservative MP was jailed for perjury in 2001 after being found guilty of lying and cheating in his 1987 libel case against the Daily Star.

To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

Watch: Jeffrey Archer spoke about his time in prison, today's politics and retirement in a BBC Breakfast interview last week

The Queen said he was "an exception to the end" and that it was "with sadness that I learned of his death yesterday, on the eve of publication of his final work and so soon after appearing at my Queen's Reading Room Festival".

Archer was a supporter of the Queen's Reading Room charity.

"My sympathies go to Mary and the family at this time of sorrow. I hope it may be some consolation for them to know what pleasure Jeffrey brought to me and to so many millions of readers through the pages of his works.

"Wherever the next page turns to, I trust there will be champagne and Shepherd's Pie in abundance. Camilla R."

Archer's parties were known for serving champagne and shepherd's pie to guests.

False alibi

Archer sold more than 300 million books in his five-decade writing career, including the Clifton Chronicles and Kane and Abel, and often set the novels in his home town of Wellington, Somerset.

In a statement, Archer's publisher HarperCollins said the author died "suddenly and peacefully at home" on Monday between writing sessions.

Archer was born in north London in 1940 but soon moved to Weston-super-Mare in Somerset and in 1969, Archer was elected MP for the Lincolnshire constituency of Louth.

He served as an MP for five years before becoming Conservative Party deputy chairman.

He moved to the House of Lords in 1992 but was jailed for four years for perjury and perverting the course of justice in 2001.

He was found to have lied in libel action he had brought against the Daily Star newspaper, in which he was awarded £500,000 in damages.

The Star had alleged Archer had slept with a sex worker.

The peer was found by the court to have perverted the course of justice by asking a former friend to give him a false alibi and producing fake diary entries to back up his story.

He was also found to have perjured himself on oath during the libel trial.

He was released from jail in 2003 and returned to the House of Lords until he retired in 2024.

Jeffrey Archer, pictured here with Margaret Thatcher, served as a Conservative MP and deputy party chairman

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch described Archer's death as "devastating news".

"We will miss him very much," she told BBC Breakfast on Tuesday, adding that he had texted her earlier on Monday.

Badenoch said he was "very much loved by the Conservative family", adding: "I'm glad that I saw him recently."

Speaking about what she described as "other parts of his life", she said: "He did serve his time, he made amends, and he wanted to do a lot of good in the world."

Former Conservative prime minister Sir John Major said "we have lost a man who lived one of the most remarkable lives of our age", and that he will be "much missed – and long remembered".

Archer's last novel, Adam and Eve, was released on Tuesday.

Broadcaster Gyles Brandreth told BBC Breakfast that he was with Archer on Sunday. "I mean, literally 72 hours ago, doing a show in the West End of London celebrating this book, the publication, and he was in great form.

"He didn't really acknowledge that he'd changed much since being in prison, but I think he became a nicer person in some ways, a gentler, a milder person after the prison experience."

Former Conservative Party leader Iain Duncan Smith described Archer as "a remarkable man who did everything at full bore", adding: "There were simply no half measures with him."

Other former ministers also paid tribute. Sajid Javid said Archer had been a "dear friend", while Sir Jeremy Hunt said Archer had "showed enormous kindness with his advice about how to become a writer".

James Cleverly said the author and politician had been "a huge personality and fantastic storyteller", and that he had been very supportive when his wife Suzie was recovering from cancer.

Reform UK member and former Conservative minister Nadim Zahawi, wrote: "Jeffrey Archer was a dear friend and an extraordinary human being. His gift for storytelling was matched by his wit, warmth and boundless energy. Life was never dull in Jeffrey's company."

Author and former politician Jeffrey Archer dies aged 86 Published 20 hours ago

Jeffrey Archer: bestselling novelist whose political career ended in scandal Published 1 day ago

Archer 'nostalgic' about Somerset before death Published 19 hours ago

Last week, Archer returned to his former school to promote his last book.

"It's wonderful to come back. What I got a real thrill about when I was walking towards the library is seeing the young boys and girls and thinking, 'that's the next generation'," Archer said at Wellington School.

Archer had been due to attend the Cheltenham Literature Festival on Saturday to discuss his final novel.

He and his wife Mary had celebrated their 60th wedding anniversary this year, HarperCollins said.

The couple have two sons and five grandchildren.

stories.summary: The Conservatives say their plan would protect the UK at a time when Nato allies have warned of Russian drone incursions.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:

Watch: Badenoch outlines 'Britannia Shield' policy

Published 5 October 2026

The Conservatives have pledged to invest £10bn in a system to defend Britain against long-range missiles and drones, if they win the next general election.

The party said the "Britannia Shield" would offer the UK an integrated network of radar, command and control systems, as well as interceptor missiles.

The Tories initially said the system would be "in essence a British 'Iron Dome'", likening it to Israel's missile shield, however party leader Kemi Badenoch drew back from the comparison in broadcast interviews.

She said the plan would be funded from within their commitment to spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030, paid for by welfare reform and reprioritisation of other spending.

Badenoch said that the £10bn cost would be split over 10 years, with £1bn allocated each year for the project.

Earlier this year, Gen Sir Richard Barrons told MPs on the Commons defence select committee "the cost of an iron dome at entry level is probably £80bn over 10 years".

Speaking to the BBC, Badenoch said: "We are not building the iron dome... we are designing something specific for the kind of threat that we face here."

She added: "It is not going to be the daily onslaught that Israel has, so we don't need that level of capability."

More on this story

Badenoch's £10bn air defence plan points to growing concern over protecting UK's skies Published 12 hours ago

What are Israel's Iron Dome and other missile shields? Published 16 October 2024

UK missiles offer may help Ukraine - but they are not what Zelensky needs most Published 24 August

The Conservative leader said she had been listening to figures like Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and following the impact of the war in Iran on Gulf countries when crafting her plans.

"There is a new type of warfare," she said, adding: "Drone warfare requires a different type of missile defence.

"We could have a situation for example where people could come in very close to the English Channel and are able to send drones and missiles at our critical national infrastructure."

Pressed on how her party would fund the spending, Badenoch said: "We are not messing around - we are very very concerned about the state not just of our defence but the state of our economy.

"We need to get serious, we need to find savings."

She said the Conservatives would find savings from the welfare budget, redirecting spending on net-zero research, reinstating the two-child benefit cap and restricting housing benefits.

"Some people may not agree with those decisions but we are making choices."

The Tories added the proposal would strengthen the UK's air defence systems at a time when Nato allies have warned they are facing repeated Russian drone incursions.

The party also cited a report from the defence committee of MPs last November which said the UK was lagging behind its European counterparts in having a plan to defend itself and overseas territories from a military attack.

The UK's existing Sky Sabre air defence system, seen in 2022 at the Royal Artillery's change of colours parade at Baker Barracks, Thorney Island

The Conservatives said the system would have three components - new advanced radar systems, upgraded command and control systems to integrate information from across Britain's defences and rapidly decide a response, and new interceptor missiles as well as counter-drone capabilities.

The three-tiered design of the proposal is similar to the British Army's current Sky Sabre , external air defence system.

This system - which can intercept munitions and aircraft as well as integrate with wider air defences - was deployed by the UK to the Middle East earlier this year for defensive action against Iranian attacks.

Sidharth Kaushal, a senior fellow at the defence and security think tank RUSI (the Royal United Services Institute), said £10bn would "probably cover" what the UK "actually needs" including horizon radar and more E-7 aircraft.

"In contrast, if what the Conservatives envision is a truly Israeli-style multi-layered missile defence system, £10bn probably wouldn't get there," he said.

"But that system would also be quite superfluous, arguably."

Prof Steven Barrett, CEO of Cambridge Aerospace which has been developing interceptor missiles, told the BBC £10bn was a "significant commitment" but the exact cost of the project would depend on the detail of the Conservatives' proposal.

He said that it would not be practical for the system to defend "every square inch" of UK territory and a more plausible setup would cover "significant parts of the population in key high density areas".

He also said there needed to be a focus on protecting critical national infrastructure, adding that a "huge amount of damage" could be done if data centres used by transport and health systems came under attack.

In his speech at the conference in Birmingham, shadow defence secretary James Cartlidge said: "With a £10bn budget, this would be one of Britain's most significant military programmes since the Cold War.

"But one that is totally necessary because of the threats we face."

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said in response: "They [the Conservatives] cut the Army to its smallest size since Napoleon and left a £17bn hole in the equipment plan.

"Their own defence secretary, Ben Wallace, admitted our Armed Forces had been 'hollowed out and underfunded'."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has been under pressure to set out how he will reach Nato's 3.5% of GDP spending target by 2035, up from an estimated 2.6% this year.

The current Labour government's Defence Investment Plan includes more than £350m to double the number of Sky Sabre systems operated by the British Army, with ground-based air defence sitting alongside air and maritime capabilities.

stories.title: I won't accept exclusion within Green Party, says Polanski after criticism of Zionism motion
stories.summary: Labour MPs and the European Greens have demanded clarity from the Green Party over a "Zionism is racism" motion.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Green Party leader Zack Polanski did not take part in the vote on Sunday

Published 5 October 2026

Zack Polanski has said he will not accept anyone being excluded from the Green Party "because of the religious or communal body they are part of", after members adopted a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism.

The Green leader said "no-one will be made unwelcome because of their background, their faith, or where they worship".

The motion defines Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine".

More than a dozen Labour MPs reported the Greens to the equality watchdog on Monday, saying it raised "serious questions".

A Green Party spokesperson said: "We remain committed to upholding our own Code of Conduct and our duties under the Equality Act, and to ensuring the Green Party continues to be a safe place for all members."

Tensions exposed among Greens by 'Zionism is racism' conference vote Published 1 day ago

Nine Labour MPs have also referred the party to Sussex Police, asking the force to investigate whether alleged "possible antisemitic offences" at the conference merit a criminal investigation.

A spokesperson for Sussex Police said: "We can confirm we have received a letter and are reviewing its contents to determine the appropriate next steps."

It is the latest development in a backlash to the policy motion , which was put forward by a group of activists at the party's conference in Brighton and endorsed by 1,022 votes to 813.

"The real, material, manifestation of Zionism has been the historic and ongoing dehumanisation, displacement, dispossession, disenfranchisement and destruction of Palestinians," it said.

The motion has exposed divisions between the party's newly enlarged membership base under leader Zack Polanski and its MPs elected at the last general election.

Polanski did not take part in the vote on Sunday and four of the party's five MPs opposed it.

Israel's foreign ministry responded by banning Polanski from entering the country, while some Jewish groups have described it as an "attack on the Jewish community".

In his first comments since the motion was passed, having declined interviews on Monday, Polanski released a lengthy statement saying he "take[s] seriously my responsibility to make sure everyone feels safe and welcome in our party".

He added: "As leader I will not accept any exclusion, or refusal to engage with anyone, because of the religious or communal body they are part of."

He said his party and its leadership stood for "deeply held values of compassion, fairness and equality for all".

Polanski, who is Jewish, added that "antisemitism and criticism of the Israeli state are, and must always be, completely distinct".

European Greens distance themselves

On Monday, a group of Labour MPs wrote two letters to the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) - organised by former Home Office minister Mike Tapp - raising concerns about the motion, and amendments to protect Jewish members attending Zionist synagogues being voted down.

"Taken together, these developments raise serious questions about whether Jewish members can participate freely and equally in the party, and whether their religious and communal connections could expose them to complaints or disciplinary action," their letter to the watchdog said.

The EHRC, which regulates equality law in Great Britain, previously found failings in how Labour handled antisemitism.

In a statement, the EHRC told the BBC it would "consider each complaint carefully" and had not at this stage launched an investigation.

It added: "We have guidance advising political parties on their responsibilities under the Equality Act 2010. Like all duty-bearers, political parties must comply with the Act and take steps to avoid discrimination."

The European Green Party, of which the Green Party for England and Wales is a member, released a statement on Monday saying it wanted to "unequivocally distance" itself from the motion.

The umbrella body said it would "immediately demand clarity" from the party's leadership on how they would protect Jewish people and self-determination.

Meanwhile, Green MP Ellie Chowns told Radio 4's PM programme she was "deeply saddened" the motion had become party policy but disagreed it was antisemitic, saying it was underpinned by "principled opposition to the actions of the Israeli government".

She suggested a review of Green policymaking processes was needed since "less than 1%" of the party's more than 200,000 members had participated in the vote.

stories.body:
Wanying Zhang surveilled Taiwanese president’s son and family for China while in US, according to FBI

The FBI arrested a woman at Los Angeles international airport (LAX) as she was leaving the country and accused her of spying on the Taiwan president’s family for China .

Wanying Zhang, also know as Heather, surveilled the Taiwanese president’s son and his family for the Chinese government while in the United States, according to the FBI.

Zhang, 34, was arrested on charges for working for China without registering as a foreign agent as legally required, first assistant US state attorney Bill Essayli of California’s central federal district announced on social media. Zhang took photos and videos of her targets and sent license plate information to Chinese officials, he said.

Citing real-estate licensing and listing records, the Los Angeles news outlet KTLA reported that Zhang was a licensed real-estate salesperson based in the southern California city of Irvine.

She was arrested as she was departing for a flight to China . Her nationality was not clear, and it was also not immediately clear if she had an attorney representing her.

She was due to appear on Monday in federal court in Los Angeles .

Taiwan’s presidential office confirmed relatives of the Taiwanese president, Lai Ching-te were the targets. The office did not specify if it was the president’s son, saying that “this is a classic case of transnational repression”.

“Taiwan condemns in the strongest terms such barbaric acts – which disregard human rights and national sovereignty and aim to suppress, threaten, or even harm individuals advocating for freedom and democracy or their families – as such behavior should not be tolerated in the civilized world,” spokesperson Karen Kuo said in a statement.

The Chinese embassy in the US did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday. And the foreign ministry in Beijing was closed for holidays.

Taiwan and China split after a civil war in 1949. But China claims the island as part of its own territory.

Lai, who was voted into office in 2024, has said that Taiwan and China do not belong to each other. He also has said the “People’s Republic of China has no right to represent Taiwan”.

China considers Lai a separatist and has called him a “destroyer of peace”.

While in office, Lai has stepped up spending on defense for Taiwan – notably pledging to increase defense spending from 3% to 5% of the GDP, and pushing through a special budget for the construction of a T-Dome air defense system.

stories.title: MPs call for investigation after Lutnick-Epstein whistleblower dies
stories.summary: Simon Andriesz said he felt let down by the UK's Financial Conduct Authority before his death last month.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Simon Andriesz, a former senior employee of BGC Partners, died last month in Thailand

Published 6 October 2026

The treatment of whistleblowers by the UK's financial watchdog must be investigated following the death of a British trader who exposed evidence of links between US commerce secretary Howard Lutnick and Jeffrey Epstein, MPs have said.

Simon Andriesz, a former senior employee of BGC Partners - the international firm of financial brokers founded and run by Lutnick before his appointment by US President Donald Trump - died last month in Thailand.

Earlier this year, Andriesz raised concerns with the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), the FBI and other watchdogs about evidence he had uncovered of business links between Epstein and Lutnick. It cast doubt on Lutnick's public statements about his associations with the late sex offender.

A group of UK MPs have now said his death raises "deeply troubling questions" about the way whistleblowers can be treated when they approach the FCA - the financial regulator - with concerns about wrongdoing and subsequent retaliation.

Andriesz's family said he had taken his own life on 23 September, and that there was no suggestion of foul play.

How US commerce secretary's Epstein links were uncovered by British whistleblower Published 14 July

Andriesz uncovered evidence that Lutnick had sought, in Andriesz's words, to "buy a prince", offering to go into business with Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor in 2013 and utilise the former prince's contacts to attract investments, in exchange for a loan of £1m. BGC told the BBC the proposed joint venture did not go ahead.

Andriesz also submitted evidence to the FCA to support his allegations of misconduct at Lutnick's former firm, including an allegation that cash from the pool of commission money set aside to pay brokers' bonuses was "embezzled" for improper purposes – an allegation the firm has denied.

Epstein Files: Lutnick, the Royals and the British Whistleblower

A former trader reveals how he unearthed evidence that US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had failed to disclose a business relationship with the paedophile financier Jeffrey Epstein.

Listen now on BBC Sounds

Weeks before his death, Andriesz told a public event led by MPs, whistleblowers and campaigners calling for fairer regulation that he felt "thoroughly let down" and had been put through "absolute hell" by the FCA, to whom he had sent evidence of what he regarded as whistleblower retaliation by BGC and its lawyers.

The FCA had previously told Andriesz there was "insufficient evidence" to conclude there had been retaliation, a conclusion he believed made it harder to win a claim against BGC at tribunal.

BGC previously told the BBC it had strong policies protecting whistleblowers and denied retaliating against him.

A 2012 snapshot discovered in the Epstein files shows Lutnick (right) and Epstein (centre) on Little St James

John McDonnell, the Labour backbench MP and chair of the All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) on Investment Fraud and Fairer Financial Services, described Andriesz's death as a "profound and preventable tragedy".

He said whistleblowers were "an essential part of the financial regulatory system" and warned there would be consequences for the integrity of the system if people did not believe they would be "treated properly, protected appropriately and listened to seriously".

The group of MPs called for the FCA to pay for an independent party to evaluate its handling of whistleblowers.

'Extreme retaliation and devastation'

In July, Andriesz told MPs and campaigners the FCA had been fully informed about other serious allegations he had made as long ago as 2018 and accused it of inaction.

The FCA told the BBC in July it had acted on his allegations and pointed to a supervision order it had issued based on his information.

But in Andriesz's view that amounted to little more than a regulatory "slap on the wrist" and made it harder to make a claim for whistleblower retaliation against BGC at tribunal.

Later that month, he told a meeting of the campaign group the Transparency Task Force the FCA was not fulfilling its obligations to the public and whistleblowers and merely "pays lip service" to the rules and regulations.

"It protects the institution and then exposes the whistleblower to extreme retaliation and devastation to their lives and families," he said.

The FCA told the BBC it was appointing a new non-executive director on its board, former Bank of England director Lea Paterson, to conduct a review into Andriesz's treatment and the FCA's handling of his whistleblower allegations.

An FCA spokesperson said: "We are very sorry to hear of Mr Andriesz's death. Our thoughts are with his family and friends.

"Since expressing our condolences, we'd asked Lea Paterson, who has just joined our board as a non-executive director, to review how we interacted with Mr Andriesz to learn any lessons for the future."

Jeremy Clarkson: Farming this year was 'an absolute disaster'

Published 5 October 2026

Jeremy Clarkson has said it had been a "terrible" year for farming due to the hot weather, at a surprise appearance at the Conservative Party conference in Birmingham.

The former Top Gear presenter and star of Clarkson's Farm also said farmers were being "attacked" from every angle by rising costs, but he was optimistic about the future.

He was greeted by loud applause from the Tory faithful, but joked that "a lot of people have come dressed as seats, I notice, around the edges there".

In a question and answer session alongside land agent Charlie Ireland, he also criticised the economic conditions faced by business owners, asking: "Why would anybody set up a business in this country right now?"

Clarkson - who also hosts ITV's Who Wants to be a Millionaire - was introduced to the stage by the Conservative shadow environment secretary Victoria Atkins.

Asked what kind of year he had had on the farm, Clarkson said: "We worked really hard all year and we ended up with, I think I'm right in saying, three ounces of hen food.

"It was an absolute disaster on the farming side but, I mean, luckily we've got other projects going on now.

"But the farming is very, very difficult – very, very difficult at the moment."

He added: "I'm very fortunate that I do have other income streams and newspaper columns, but if you're an ordinary farmer, it's not just the weather.

"Remember, it's as Charlie was saying, the attacks come from everywhere – whether it's Iran or Ukraine or taxes or energy costs – whatever it might be, it's just relentless."

The TV presenter has long been a Conservative supporter and was involved in the campaign against the Labour government's inheritance tax plans for farmers .

Former chancellor Rachel Reeves announced the government would levy inheritance tax on family farms in the party's first budget.

But the plan was watered down last year following the farmers' campaign and pressure from some of Labour's rural MPs.

Responding to Clarkson's comments, a government source said: "We are working with farmers to strengthen domestic food production and make supply chains more resilient as we build a stronger and more profitable farming sector together."

Clarkson also joked about comments by Labour MP Jenny Riddell-Carpenter who said the Britain of country pubs and black Labradors was a "nostalgic" false memory.

He joked that he was a "socialist" because he drinks lager and has two fox red Labradors, after it was reported Riddell-Carpenter told a Labour conference fringe event she feared the far right deciding what the vision of rural areas is.

Riddell-Carpenter had said: "It'll be that warm ale, a black Labrador by your feet in a pub that doesn't exist, and with symbolism of fox hunting all around them. It'll be a very far-right nostalgic vision of Britain that we don't want to have, (that) never really existed."

O'Neill said she was "proud" to stand with the residents and "will continue to stand with them"

Published 5 October 2026

First Minister Michelle O'Neill has dismissed a call from the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) to resign over her role in protests against the Drumcree parade.

The Sinn Féin vice-president was branded the "first minister of lawlessness" as unionists criticised the demonstrations on Garvaghy Road.

Police are investigating the unlawful protests which blocked an Orange Order march from passing along the mainly nationalist street in Portadown, County Armagh.

Facing questions in the Stormont assembly, O'Neill said she was "proud" to stand with the residents and "will continue to stand with them".

She described the planned Orange march on 27 September as "unwanted, sectarian and triumphalist".

O'Neill was speaking on Monday in response to an urgent question on the Drumcree dispute tabled by DUP assembly member Phillip Brett.

O'Neill returns to Garvaghy Road as police investigate Sunday's 'unlawful protest' Published 6 days ago

Court of Appeal reserves judgement over Drumcree parade dispute Published 1 day ago

An uneasy peace – how a week of the Drumcree parade dispute has unfolded Published 4 days ago

Michelle O'Neill was speaking in response to an urgent question from DUP MLA Phillip Brett

He called on O'Neill to "drop the bravado" and claimed she had shown "utter contempt" for the ministerial pledge of office.

Brett continued: "If you have been found to breach the ministerial code or the law, will you do the decent thing for once and resign as first minister?"

The first minister responded: "Catch yourself on, would be where I would start with that one.

"I'm going to continue to turn up for the people of the Garvaghy Road.

"I'm proud to stand with them and I will continue to stand with them."

Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) assembly member Timothy Gaston accused O'Neill of being the "first minister of lawlessness" over her role in the street protests.

O'Neill replied: "I am the first minister of what is right."

She added that "we won't need to AI it" - a reference to a TUV councillor who posted online an AI image which exaggerated the size of a loyalist rally in Portadown.

DUP assembly member Jonathan Buckley questioned whether O'Neill would "accept and abide by the lawful decision of the courts" when appeal court judges make a ruling on the parade dispute.

Protesters along the Garvaghy Road, with the road blocked at a number of points on 27 September

The first minister said that "when the law is wrong I will stand firmly against it" and described the planned march as "morally wrong".

O'Neill later said "shame on you" to DUP assembly members over the party's handling of the Drumcree dispute.

"Your party has championed this," she said to DUP members on the opposite benches.

O'Neill flatly rejected a claim from Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) leader Jon Burrows that many people now regarded the first minister as "completely morally bankrupt".

Earlier, Stormont Speaker Edwin Poots raised concerns over the first minister not attending the chamber last week to answer the tabled urgent question.

The DUP assembly member said O'Neill's absence last Monday was "discourteous" to the assembly and the public.

"Members know my views on ministers being accountable to this house on behalf of the people who put us all here," he said.
